title: Heavy metal contamination of mining fields in North-Central Nigeria
author: Orosun, Inuyomi, et al.

steps.title: Collect and label soil samples
steps.instruction: Collect 72 soil samples (36 from Ifelodun beryllium field and 36 from Moro gold field) in duplicate using a soil auger; place each sample (~2 kg) into a black polyethylene bag and label each bag for easy identification.

substeps.instruction: Collect duplicates with a soil auger.
Put each ~2 kg sample into a black polyethylene bag.

steps.title: Dry, pulverize, and sieve soil
steps.instruction: Air‑dry the collected soils in an open room until a constant dry weight is reached; pulverise the dried soil and pass it through a 1 mm sieve.

steps.title: Digest soil sample with acids
steps.instruction: Weigh 1 g of sieved soil into a digestion flask; add 3 mL concentrated HNO₃ and 9 mL concentrated HCl; heat on an electrical heating plate to boiling for approximately 15 minutes until brownish fumes cease, confirming complete digestion; allow the digest to cool.

substeps.instruction: Weigh 1 g soil into digestion flask.
Heat to boiling for ~15 min until fumes stop.

steps.title: Filter and dilute digested extract
steps.instruction: Filter the cooled digest into a 25 mL volumetric (standard) flask; rinse the filter with a few millilitres of distilled water and bring the final volume to the mark with distilled water.

steps.title: Prepare calibration standards and blanks
steps.instruction: Obtain 1000 ppm standard solutions of each potentially toxic element from Inorganic Ventures; prepare 100 ppm stock solutions by diluting the 1000 ppm standards using C₁V₁=C₂V₂ to a final volume of 100 mL; from each 100 ppm stock, prepare working standards covering the linear range of the AAS using the same dilution equation; prepare blank samples with distilled water to correct reagent and water background.

substeps.instruction: Prepare 100 ppm stock: dilute 1000 ppm standard (C₁V₁=C₂V₂) to 100 mL.
Prepare working standards from the 100 ppm stock as needed.
Prepare blank samples with distilled water.

steps.title: Clean glassware and equipment
steps.instruction: Wash all laboratory apparatuses several times and rinse with de‑ionised water before each use.

steps.title: Measure metal concentrations by AAS
steps.instruction: Analyze the diluted extracts, standards, and blanks using a Buck Scientific Atomic Absorption Spectrophotometer Model 210 VGP; record concentrations; note detection limits ranging from 0.005 ppm (As) to 0.080 ppm (Pb); verify accuracy and precision using reagent blanks and duplicate samples.

description: The study focused on the measurement of the concentration of heavy metals herein referred to as potentially toxic elements (PTEs), in the samples of soil obtained from beryllium minefields and gold minefields in Ifelodun and Moro respectively, Kwara, Nigeria. The potentially toxic metals includes; Arsenic (As), Zinc (Zn), Cadmium (Cd), Nickel (Ni), Iron (Fe), Chromium (Cr), Manganese (Mn), Magnesium (Mg), Lead (Pb) and Copper (Cu). The soil samples were collected in duplicates using soil auger and packaged in a labelled polyethylene bags to avoid material reaction. The soil samples collected were digested by adding 3 ml of HNO3 and 9 ml of concentrated HCl. The solution was now heated on an electrical heating plate to boiling point for approximately 15 min. The digested solution was further filtered into standard flasks and then diluted with few ml of distilled water. The digested samples were measured into a plastic reagent bottle for Atomic Absorption Spectrophotometry. Mining and mineral processing activities is widely believed to be associated with introduction and enhancement of potentially toxic elements in the environment [1], [2], [3], [4], [5], [6], [7]. Amongst these toxic elements, Arsenic (As), Zinc (Zn), Cadmium (Cd), Nickel (Ni), Iron (Fe), Chromium (Cr), Manganese (Mn), Magnesium (Mg), Lead (Pb) and Copper (Cu) receives universal attention because their presence in the human system is reported to bring about health effects manifesting differing symptoms, subject to the nature and amount of the chemical element ingested [1,2]. When the presence of these toxic elements in the environment are enhanced by the mining activities, they will be introduced into the human system either by ingestion, inhalation or dermal contact [1], [2], [3], [4], [5], [6], [7]. Thus, data generated in this study could be used as baseline data for reference and future study of the level of potentially toxic elements contamination in soil of the mining regions.
